lessons.title: Returns, Volatility, and Distributions: The Building Blocks of Risk Modeling

children.text: Before you can compute a VaR figure using any method, historical simulation, parametric, or Monte Carlo, you have to make three quiet decisions: how you define a return, how you estimate volatility, and what distribution you assume returns follow. Get any of these wrong and the VaR number that comes out the other end, no matter how correctly you apply the formula, will be wrong too. This lesson builds the three inputs the next chapter's methods all share.

Whether you pull historical prices from NSE's bhavcopy archives, BSE's historical data portal, or a paid data vendor, the raw close-to-close price series is just simple returns waiting to be calculated. A simple return is the percentage change in price. A log return is the natural logarithm of the price ratio. For small daily moves the two are nearly identical, for large moves they diverge, and quant risk models almost always use log returns.

body.caption: Simple return: the percentage change in price.
Log return: the natural log of the price ratio. A stock falling from Rs 100 to Rs 97 has a simple return of exactly -3.000% but a log return of -3.046%, close but not identical.

body.text: Log returns are time-additive: the log return over 5 days is just the sum of the 5 daily log returns. Simple returns do not add up that cleanly, you have to compound them multiplicatively instead. That additivity is exactly why Monte Carlo simulation, which builds up multi-day paths one step at a time, is almost always built on log returns rather than simple ones.

cells: Actual percentage gain or loss on the position
Add directly, day 1 plus day 2 plus day 3
Statistical modeling, Monte Carlo simulation, volatility estimation

children.text: Estimating Volatility: Past Is Prologue, Sort Of

markDefs.definition: A volatility estimate that weights recent returns more heavily than older ones, using a decay factor lambda, so it reacts faster to changing market conditions than a simple equal-weighted average.

children.text: The simplest volatility estimate, a plain standard deviation over your lookback window, weights every day equally. A return from fourteen months ago counts exactly as much as yesterday's return. That is rarely what you want on a trading desk, where risk conditions can shift within days. The industry-standard alternative, popularized by JPMorgan's RiskMetrics framework in the 1990s and still widely used, is the

body.caption: EWMA volatility. Today's variance is a weighted blend of yesterday's variance and yesterday's squared return, controlled by the decay factor lambda.

stats.label: RiskMetrics daily lambda
stats.context: Standard decay factor for daily volatility estimation

stats.label: RiskMetrics monthly lambda
stats.context: Slower decay, more weight on older data, used for longer horizons

stats.label: Effect of a lower lambda
stats.context: Recent shocks dominate the estimate sooner

body.code:
def ewma_volatility(prev_vol, last_return, lam=0.94):
    """Update EWMA volatility given yesterday's vol and return."""
    new_var = lam * prev_vol**2 + (1 - lam) * last_return**2
    return new_var ** 0.5

# Example: prev daily vol 1.0%, a sharp -3% day just happened
updated_vol = ewma_volatility(prev_vol=0.01, last_return=-0.03)
print(f"Updated EWMA volatility: {updated_vol:.3%}")
body.caption: A single sharp move updates EWMA volatility immediately, unlike a simple equal-weighted average, which would barely move until that one day rolls out of the lookback window.

body.title: Simple Historical Std Dev vs EWMA

columns.label: Simple Historical Standard Deviation
points: Every day in the lookback window weighted equally
Slow to react to a sudden regime change
Can understate risk right after a shock, and overstate it long after one has passed

columns.label: EWMA
points: Recent days weighted more heavily via the decay factor lambda
Reacts within a day or two to a volatility spike
One parameter, lambda, to choose and justify
Basis for JPMorgan's original RiskMetrics VaR system

children.text: Choosing a Distribution: Normal, Student-t, or the Data Itself

The last lesson showed that Nifty returns have fatter tails than a normal distribution predicts. There are three broad ways to handle this once you are building a VaR model, and each one becomes a different VaR method in the next chapter. Assume returns are normal anyway, and accept that your VaR will understate tail risk. Assume a fatter-tailed distribution, like the Student-t distribution, which has an extra parameter controlling exactly how fat the tails are. Or skip assuming a distribution altogether and use the actual historical returns, tails and all, as your model. screener.in's beta figures and most retail-facing volatility numbers use the first approach. Serious risk desks rarely do.

body.caption: How today's distribution choice becomes next chapter's VaR method

cells: Symmetric, thin tails, fully described by mean and volatility
A tunable extra parameter for tail thickness
A variant of parametric VaR, or the distribution used inside Monte Carlo VaR
No assumption, use the empirical data directly
Whatever shape the actual historical returns happen to have

body.text: Window length is its own trade-off, separate from which distribution you pick. A short lookback window, say 6 months, reacts fast to new conditions but is noisy and can be dominated by one or two extreme days. A long window, say 5 years, is stable but can be stale, still pricing in a volatility regime the market has already left behind. There is no universally correct answer, only a choice you have to justify and monitor.

body.title: Update an EWMA Volatility Estimate
body.prompt: Yesterday's EWMA daily volatility estimate was 1.0%. Yesterday's return was -3%. Using RiskMetrics lambda of 0.94, what is today's updated EWMA volatility, as a percentage?
body.explanation: New variance = 0.94 x (0.01)^2 + 0.06 x (0.03)^2 = 0.000094 + 0.000054 = 0.000148. Taking the square root gives approximately 1.217%, rounded to 1.22%. Notice how much a single -3% day moves the estimate compared to a simple equal-weighted average.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: A risk manager wants a VaR model that makes no assumption at all about the shape of the return distribution, tails included. Which building block choice does this correspond to?
options: Student-t distribution with simple historical volatility
Using the empirical historical return series directly, with no distributional assumption
Log returns instead of simple returns
body.explanation: Using the actual historical returns as-is, without fitting them to any theoretical distribution, is the defining feature of Historical Simulation VaR, the first method covered in the next chapter.

body.text: Every VaR method is the same question asked with different building blocks: which return definition, which volatility estimator, which distribution assumption. Learn the blocks once, and the next chapter's three methods stop looking like three unrelated formulas.

points: Log returns are time-additive and are the standard choice for quant risk modeling, especially Monte Carlo simulation, even though simple returns are what actually shows up in your P&L.
EWMA volatility weights recent returns more heavily using a decay factor lambda, reacting to new information faster than a simple equal-weighted standard deviation.

How you handle fat tails, ignore them with a normal distribution, model them with something like a Student-t distribution, or sidestep the question with historical data, directly determines which VaR method you end up building.
Lookback window length is an independent trade-off from distribution choice: short windows react fast but are noisy, long windows are stable but can be stale.
